Heritage walk · Delhi

Heritage walk in Delhi: historical places, routes and museums

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

A heritage walk in Delhi takes you through about 3,000 years of settlement, from Painted Grey Ware levels at Purana Qila to the Sultanate cities of the south, Mughal Shahjahanabad and the colonial capital. The city has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Qutb Minar, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort Complex) and dozens of walkable precincts.

We arrange Delhi heritage walks on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Delhi matters for Indian history

Few capitals have been rebuilt as often as Delhi. Rulers moved the centre of power across the same triangle of land between the Aravalli ridge and the Yamuna again and again, and each move left walls, mosques, tombs, step wells and reservoirs that still stand among modern neighbourhoods. That is why a walk here is less about one monument and more about reading layers: an Ashokan pillar re-erected by a Tughlaq sultan, a Lodi tomb inside a 1930s garden, a Mughal gateway beside a metro station.

The usual shorthand is the seven cities of Delhi, a list that runs from Qila Rai Pithora and Mehrauli to Shahjahanabad. Historians now count more than seven, and the list leaves out the ancient settlement at Purana Qila and the colonial city of New Delhi, but it is a useful way to organise a series of walks.

Layers of Delhi's history, period by period

Excavations at Purana Qila have found Painted Grey Ware pottery of the early first millennium BCE, and later Mauryan, Shunga, Kushana and Gupta levels. An Ashokan rock edict survives at Srinivaspuri in south Delhi, and two Ashokan pillars were brought to the city in the 14th century by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.

The Tomar and Chauhan Rajput rulers held the Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora area in the 11th and 12th centuries. After 1192 the Delhi Sultanate built over it: the Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque under Qutbuddin Aibak and Iltutmish, Siri under Alauddin Khalji, Tughlaqabad and Jahanpanah under the Tughlaqs, Firozabad on the river under Firoz Shah, and garden tombs under the Sayyids and Lodis. The Delhi Sultanate guide sets out this sequence.

The Mughals and the Sur interlude gave Delhi Purana Qila, Humayun's Tomb, the tombs around Nizamuddin and, from 1639, Shah Jahan's walled city of Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid. After 1857 the British reshaped the old city, and from 1911 to 1931 built New Delhi to the designs of Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker.

Places a heritage walk in Delhi covers

  1. Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque 1192 to 14th century

    Look at the reused temple pillars in the mosque cloister, the iron pillar of the Gupta period, and the change of style between the minar's storeys.

  2. Mehrauli Archaeological Park 12th to 19th century

    Jamali Kamali, Balban's tomb with an early true arch, Rajon ki Baoli and Quli Khan's tomb in one walk.

  3. Sultan Ghari 1231

    Tomb of Iltutmish's son Nasiruddin Mahmud, usually called the first monumental Islamic tomb in India.

  4. Hauz Khas about 1295 and 1352

    Alauddin Khalji's reservoir and the madrasa and tomb added by Firoz Shah Tughlaq on its banks.

  5. Tughlaqabad Fort 1321 to 1325

    Massive sloping walls of the third city, with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb across the causeway.

  6. Begumpur Mosque 14th century

    A large congregational mosque of Jahanpanah, still standing among village houses.

  7. Firoz Shah Kotla 1354

    Ruins of Firozabad with an Ashokan pillar brought from Topra, inscribed in Brahmi.

  8. Purana Qila 1530s to 1540s, site from about 1000 BCE

    Sher Shah's Qila-i-Kuhna mosque, the Sher Mandal and excavated trenches showing earlier levels.

  9. Nizamuddin Dargah 14th century onward

    Shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya (died 1325), with the graves of Amir Khusrau and Jahanara nearby.

  10. Humayun's Tomb about 1565 to 1572

    The first great Mughal garden tomb, a UNESCO site, with Isa Khan's tomb and Arab Serai next door.

  11. Lodhi Garden 15th to 16th century

    Tombs of Muhammad Shah Sayyid and Sikandar Lodi, and the Bara Gumbad mosque group, set in a 1936 park.

  12. Safdarjung's Tomb 1754

    A late Mughal garden tomb that shows how the Humayun's Tomb model changed over two centuries.

  13. Red Fort 1639 to 1648

    Shah Jahan's palace fortress, a UNESCO site, with the Diwan-i-Am, Diwan-i-Khas and later British barracks.

  14. Jama Masjid 1650 to 1656

    Shah Jahan's congregational mosque on a raised plinth, looking down on the markets of Shahjahanabad.

  15. Kashmere Gate 1835, fighting of 1857

    Gate in the city wall stormed by British troops in September 1857, near St James' Church and the old Residency.

  16. India Gate 1921 to 1931

    Lutyens' war memorial at the end of Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath), the axis of New Delhi.

Walking routes in Delhi

Mehrauli on foot

About 3 hours

Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque → Mehrauli Archaeological Park

Nizamuddin, Humayun's Tomb and Lodhi Garden

About 3 to 4 hours, a short cab ride to Lodhi Garden

Nizamuddin Dargah → Humayun's Tomb → Lodhi Garden

Shahjahanabad

About 3 hours, metro or auto to Kashmere Gate

Red Fort → Jama Masjid → Kashmere Gate

Museums in Delhi

  • National Museum, Janpath. Harappan, Mauryan, Gupta and medieval galleries; the best place in Delhi to see the whole sequence in objects.
  • National Crafts Museum and Hasta Kala Academy. Village architecture, textiles and living craft traditions from across India.
  • Red Fort museums. ASI galleries inside the fort on the Mughal court, 1857 and the freedom struggle.
  • Purana Qila site museum. Pottery and finds from the excavations, from Painted Grey Ware to the Mughal period.

Best time for a walk

October to March, ideally in the morning. Summer walks should start by 8 am and be kept short.

Delhi heritage walks by area

Talaash Heritage runs more than 40 Delhi walks, each of them a focused visit of about two to three hours with an archaeologist or historian. Grouped by area, they let a school or company build a series across a term or a year.

Mehrauli and the Qutb: start with the Qutb complex and Mehrauli Archaeological Park, then go deeper with Rajon ki Baoli, Adham Khan's Tomb, Jahaz Mahal and Hauz-i-Shamsi, Mehrauli village and Zafar Mahal and the early tomb at Sultan Ghari.

The Sultanate cities of south Delhi: Hauz Khas, the Siri Fort area, Chor Minar, Bijay Mandal and Jahanpanah, Begumpur Mosque, Khirki Mosque, Satpula, Tughlaqabad Fort and Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb.

Nizamuddin and Humayun's Tomb: Humayun's Tomb, the Nizamuddin Dargah precinct, Isa Khan's Tomb, Nila Gumbad and Arab Serai, Sunder Nursery, Rahim's Tomb and Chausath Khamba.

Central Delhi: Purana Qila, Lodhi Garden with the Bara Gumbad and Shish Gumbad lab, Safdarjung's Tomb, Agrasen ki Baoli, Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate and Kartavya Path and the National Crafts Museum.

Shahjahanabad and the river: the Red Fort Complex, Jama Masjid and Shahjahanabad, Fatehpuri Masjid, Ghalib ki Haveli, Delhi Gate and Daryaganj and Firoz Shah Kotla.

North Delhi and 1857: Kashmere Gate, St James' Church, Nicholson Cemetery and Roshanara Bagh. For a single overview, the Delhi through seven cities study tour links the main capitals over several days.

What you see on a walk

A good Delhi walk trains the eye. At the Qutb you compare the carved bands of the minar with the reused temple pillars in the mosque cloister. At Tughlaqabad you read sloping rubble walls built for defence. At Humayun's Tomb you see the double dome, the char bagh garden and the red sandstone and white marble that later shaped the Taj Mahal. In Shahjahanabad you follow how a planned Mughal city became a dense market town of havelis, katras and mohallas.

Inscriptions, coins and building materials are part of most walks. Students learn to tell rubble masonry from dressed stone, a true arch from a corbelled one, and a Lodi dome from a Mughal one.

Delhi heritage walks for schools and colleges

For schools, the most practical walks are in enclosed, ticketed sites with toilets and shade: the Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb, Purana Qila, Safdarjung's Tomb and Sunder Nursery. Old Delhi lanes suit older students in small groups with extra adult supervision. Winter mornings from November to February are best; in summer, start by 8 am and keep walks under two hours.

Each walk can be matched to the syllabus: the Sultanate for Class 7 history, the Mughals and architecture for Classes 7 and 12, 1857 for Class 8, and urban planning for geography. A classroom lecture before the visit helps; see Museums and the stories objects tell or the Indian history timeline. Check ASI rules on group entry and photography before you go.

How we run this

  • Schools: a two-hour walk at the Qutb, Humayun's Tomb or Purana Qila, matched to the Class 7 or 12 syllabus.
  • Companies: a morning walk in Mehrauli or Sunder Nursery as a team outing.
  • Families and private groups: a walk through Old Delhi or Nizamuddin with an archaeologist or historian.

Questions people ask

Which are the best historical places in Delhi for a first heritage walk?

Start with the Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort, the three UNESCO sites. Then add Purana Qila for the ancient layers, Mehrauli Archaeological Park for the Sultanate, and Shahjahanabad for the Mughal city. Each works as a two to three hour walk.

How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Delhi?

Three: Qutb Minar and its Monuments, and Humayun's Tomb (both inscribed in 1993), and the Red Fort Complex (2007). India has 45 sites in all as of October 2026.

What is a good Delhi heritage walk for schools?

For younger students, enclosed sites such as Humayun's Tomb, the Qutb complex, Purana Qila or Sunder Nursery are easiest to manage. Older students can do Mehrauli Archaeological Park, Tughlaqabad or Old Delhi in small groups. Keep walks to two hours and go in the morning.

Which museums in Delhi are best for history?

The National Museum on Janpath covers Indian art and archaeology from the Harappan period onward. The National Crafts Museum covers living traditions, and the Red Fort museums cover the Mughals and 1857. The Purana Qila site museum shows excavated pottery.

Can a heritage walk in Delhi be done in Hindi?

Yes. Talaash Heritage walks are led by archaeologists and historians and can be held in English or Hindi, for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, on dates you choose.
